item.title: Noether's Second Theorem and the Pareto Front Structure in Multi-Criteria Variational Problems
item.description: arXiv:2611.06920v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper establishes a rigorous connection between Noether's second theorem and the structure of Pareto fronts in multi-criteria variational problems. We prove that for a family of functionals invariant under a common gauge Lie group, the regular part of the Pareto front is contained in the union of solutions to weighted Euler--Lagrange equations, and that on Pareto-optimal sections, combinations of Noether currents are conserved. Gauge symmetries are shown to impose additional constraints on the Lagrange multipliers via Bianchi-type identities, reducing the dimension of the admissible weight space. Two practical approaches are derived from this result: dimensionality reduction via gauge fixing and scalarization with penalty terms. The theory is validated on three classical problems: the linear-quadratic regulator with two criteria, a model predictive control problem with a minimax criterion, and the double integrator with control constraints. In each case, the Pareto front is shown to satisfy an exact conservation law, and the analytical structure of the front is recovered from the symmetries of the problem. The results demonstrate that gauge functions (null Lagrangians) can restore invariants even when the dynamics break the symmetry, and that control constraints do not destroy the underlying conservation laws but merely restrict the admissible set. The proposed approach yields a Pareto front with minimal deviation from the theoretical curve, outperforming known multi-objective algorithms, and provides a new foundation for the analytical treatment of multi-criteria optimization in nonlinear dynamics and control.
item.dc:creator: Evgeny Nikulchev

item.title: Ramification of Weighted Central Paths and Super-linear Interior-Point Methods for Semi-definite Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2611.07080v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The local convergence of primal-dual interior-point methods for semi-definite optimization is closely tied to the regularity of the central path at its limiting point. Without strict complementarity, the central path can exhibit fractional power asymptotics and need not be differentiable in the ordinary barrier parameter. We show that this obstruction can be removed simultaneously for a family of weighted \AHO~central paths. More precisely, there exists a common ramification exponent $N$ such that all weighted paths in a fixed neighborhood of the identity become analytic at the limiting point after the reparametrization $\mu\mapsto\mu^N$. Using higher-order derivatives of these reparametrized paths, we construct a feasible $p$th-order predictor-corrector interior-point method. Under a uniform predictor regularity condition, and without assuming strict complementarity, we prove that the normalized complementarity gaps converge with $Q$-order at least $(p+1)/\rho$, where $\rho$ is the reparametrization exponent used by the method. We also establish super-linear convergence of the simultaneously vanishing primal-dual blocks, derive an explicit quantitative reduction bound throughout the predictor regularity region, and obtain a doubly logarithmic outer iteration bound once the iterates enter the local super-linear regime. Finally, we illustrate the predicted higher-order behavior on a collection of degenerate and non-degenerate semi-definite optimization problems.
item.dc:creator: Ali Mohammad-Nezhad, Pouya Sampourmahani, Tamas Terlaky

item.title: Practical Semialgebraic Optimization via Sparse Sample-Based Sum-of-Squares Programming
item.description: arXiv:2611.07108v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As the importance of semialgebraic optimization grows in engineering, so does the need for scalable sum-of-squares (SOS) methods. Their convex relaxations can guide mixed-integer search and often deliver certified global optima outright. Scaling traditional SOS typically requires hand-crafted bases and redundant constraints, whereas sample-based SOS numerically exploits feasible set geometry to reduce bases and build smaller, often tighter relaxations from black-box evaluations. However, discrete variables can require exponentially many samples, and each sampled equation couples all cliques, destroying correlative sparsity. In this work, we avoid enumeration and slack variables by sampling a tractable variety that contains the feasible set, with multipliers only for the omitted constraints. To recover sparsity, we introduce "separator" polynomials that split the sampled equations into local systems coupled only on clique overlaps. This yields a novel, convergent hierarchy of semidefinite programs (SDPs) with block sizes and sample requirements governed by local interactions rather than total problem size. Lastly, we show how to verify sample sufficiency and prune redundant equations numerically before solving. In robust estimation and motion planning, we obtain certifiably small optimality gaps at scales far beyond those reported for traditional sparse SOS. For example, we solve a truncated least-squares 3D registration problem with 1600 candidate correspondences in under 49 seconds using an off-the-shelf SDP solver on a laptop CPU.
item.dc:creator: Jason Nezvadovitz, David M. Rosen

item.title: How to Look Inside the Black Box: A Survey of Yu. E. Nesterov's Contributions (On the Award of the 2026 Gauss Prize)
item.description: arXiv:2611.07114v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: On July 23, 2026, at the opening of the International Congress of Mathematicians in Philadelphia, the International Mathematical Union announced the award of the Gauss Prize to Yurii Evgenievich Nesterov -- an award for mathematical work with significant applications outside mathematics. This article explains the mathematical content of the recognized work of Yu. E. Nesterov and traces its influence on modern computational practice. The exposition is based on a concept that Yu. E. Nesterov himself regards as one of his main results: the classical complexity theory of convex optimization is oriented toward a black-box oracle, but its pessimistic bounds can be overcome by using a priori information about the internal structure of the objective function. We trace Yu. E. Nesterov's scientific career, then introduce the language of oracle complexity together with a classification of objective function models (geometric, algebraic, and structural), and subsequently discuss his main results in chronological order: the fast gradient method, fast automatic differentiation, the theory of self-concordant barriers and polynomial-time interior-point methods, the $\pi/2$ theorem, the stable dynamics model of traffic flows, the smoothing technique, primal-dual methods, cubic regularization of Newton's method, the modified Gauss--Newton scheme, coordinate descent methods and methods for huge-scale problems, gradient-free methods, universal gradient methods, implementable tensor methods, and "superfast" methods. Each topic is accompanied by historical background, precise statements specifying the problem class, oracle, and type of guarantee, examples, and a discussion of the current state of the art.
item.dc:creator: A. V. Gasnikov, A. Yu. Gornov, D. M. Dvinskikh, Yu. V. Dorn, D. I. Kamzolov, Yu. V. Maximov, V. V. Matyukhin, R. F. Hildebrand

item.title: Multiplayer Stopping Games with a Conditionally Atomless Filtration
item.description: arXiv:2611.07184v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Stopping games are the multiplayer generalization of optimal stopping problems, in which each player independently chooses when to stop, and the payoff depends on who stops first and when. While the existence of $\varepsilon$-equilibria in two-player stopping games with integrable payoffs is known, the multiplayer case has remained open. We prove that every multiplayer stopping game in discrete time with integrable payoff process admits an $\varepsilon$-equilibrium for every $\varepsilon > 0$, provided the filtration is conditionally atomless. This condition is satisfied, in particular, when the underlying probability space is $\{0,1\}^{\dN}$ endowed with the uniform measure and its natural filtration. Our method also shows that every three-player stopping game, without the restriction to conditionally atomless filtration, admits an $\varepsilon$-equilibrium, for every $\varepsilon > 0$. The proof combines techniques developed for two-player stopping games and for multiplayer quitting games, with a key new insight: the richness encoded in a conditionally atomless filtration can substitute for an external public randomization device, allowing players to coordinate without an explicit coordination signal.
item.dc:creator: Robert Samuel Simon, Eilon Solan, Grzegorz Tomkowicz

item.title: Cubic Optimization over Three Nonnegative Integers Is NP-hard
item.description: arXiv:2611.07269v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove that deciding whether an integer cubic polynomial takes a value at most one over three nonnegative integers is NP-hard. Hardness holds even when every feasible objective value is a positive integer, so every constructed instance has a finite, attained minimum. This establishes a sharp dimension boundary for the tractability of cubic integer optimization in fixed dimension. Our reduction from positive 1-in-3 satisfiability encodes Boolean constraints as modular conditions and uses an algebraic norm to construct a cubic objective whose minimum is one exactly for satisfiable formulas. The resulting six-parameter threshold language is NP-complete and admits short exponent certificates.
item.dc:creator: Linchuan Wei

item.title: Selecting the best UAV pursuer for minimum time moving target interception among obstacles
item.description: arXiv:2611.07279v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A team of unmanned aerial vehicles (pursuers) with different positions, headings, speeds, minimum turning radii and launch delays must respond to a target that moves at constant velocity through a region containing static circular obstacles. Only one pursuer is launched, namely the one that can intercept the target first. We present a computationally efficient, obstacle-aware interceptor-selection framework for this setting. The interception problem of each pursuer is posed as a minimum-time optimal control problem and is solved over an explicit family of candidate path types through an arc-parameterised nonlinear programme in which the obstacles are toured tangentially and every part of the path is kept out of every obstacle by exact (not sampled) distance constraints. A closed-form lower bound, obtained by relaxing the curvature and obstacle constraints, is combined with the verified feasible interception times in a bound-and-select algorithm. We prove that the pruning is certified: a pursuer is skipped only if it cannot improve the best verified interception time, so bound-and-select returns the same pursuer and the same time as solving every pursuer, and the method reports a boundary on the optimal team interception time. Numerical experiments with solver diagnostics and repeated random starts, sensitivity studies in the target speed (with the selection crossover located by bisection), the launch delay, the turning radius and the obstacle configuration, a comparison with nearest-pursuer, fastest-pursuer and straight-line-time selection rules on random scenarios, a computational comparison with full enumeration for growing team sizes, and a geographic case study show that the selected pursuer is frequently neither the nearest nor the fastest, and that lower-bound pruning removes a large part of the computational effort without changing the decision.
item.dc:creator: M. M. Rizvi, Masuda Akter

item.title: Last-Iterate Convergence of Stochastic Gradient Methods for Unbounded Problems
item.description: arXiv:2611.07334v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Last-iterate convergence guarantees for stochastic gradient methods have attracted significant attention as practical implementations typically return the last iterate instead of an average of the iterates. In this paper, we study two approaches for analyzing the last-iterate convergence of proximal and projected stochastic gradient methods without bounded domain or bounded variance assumptions, where black-box variational inference serves as a running example. Under two related assumptions relaxing the bounded variance, we show near-optimal anytime rate $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(1/\sqrt{T})$ for the last iterate. Moreover, when the horizon $T$ is known, we remove the logarithmic factor and obtain the optimal order $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{T})$, matching the order known under bounded variance or bounded domain assumptions.
item.dc:creator: Kevin Kurian Thomas Vaidyan, Ahmet Alacaoglu, Michael P. Friedlander

item.title: From What Is Used to What Is Missing: Rethinking Dynamic Rank in LoRA
item.description: arXiv:2611.07349v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning with LoRA is governed by rank, which controls parameter budget and locally accessible task updates. Existing dynamic-rank methods mainly focus on capacity allocation, leaving unresolved whether the current adaptation space is sufficient for the task. We characterize the first-order information boundary of standard factor gradients, showing that their unobservable subspace coincides with the normal space of the low-rank manifold. Thus, factor gradients alone cannot distinguish under-optimization within the current space from task-relevant directions beyond its first-order reach. This motivates a geometric view of rank evolution, where tangent information optimizes existing degrees of freedom and the normal spectrum quantifies the value of new ones. Under a local quadratic model, we show that leading normal singular directions yield the locally optimal rank expansion, with spectral energy determining its gain. Building on this characterization, we propose GEAR, which turns the tangent--normal decomposition into rank evolution through tangent-space optimization, matrix-free normal-spectrum estimation for rank expansion, and task-induced geometric initialization. Across language and vision benchmarks, GEAR achieves the best average performance in all evaluated settings with substantially fewer trainable parameters. On LLaMA3-8B, it raises the average commonsense score from 86.61 to 88.45 while reducing trainable parameters from 42.0M to 14.4M.
item.dc:creator: Peng Xue, Guodong Fan, Guang-Yong Chen, Xing Chen

item.title: Continuous-time q-Learning for Finite-Horizon Portfolio Choice with Optimal Stopping in Jump-Diffusion Markets
item.description: arXiv:2611.07362v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a structured continuous-time q-learning framework for finite-horizon investment and optimal stopping under jump-diffusion dynamics with unknown parameters. A penalty approximation transforms the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman variational inequality into an HJB equation with a binary control for the stopping penalty. An auxiliary state incorporates the resulting control-dependent discount factor into a Markovian formulation. We randomize controls on the mixed action space and introduce Shannon entropy regularization, establishing policy improvement and martingale characterizations of the continuous-time q-function. These results motivate a structured q-learning algorithm that constructs the q-function from the penalty HJB equation and jointly learns the value function and unknown generator parameters from sample paths. We apply the method to portfolio choice with optimal stopping in a simulation study. We further conduct a two-asset empirical study, evaluating learned strategies on bootstrap paths from held-out test returns versus an MLE-finite difference benchmark.
item.dc:creator: Tingting Zhang, Can Yang

item.title: Random Reshuffling for Smooth Convex Optimization: Dominates Stochastic Gradient Descent
item.description: arXiv:2611.07406v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) is one of the most classical optimization algorithms with favorable theoretical guarantees, yet its practical implementation differs subtly from its well-known form and is often referred to as Shuffling Stochastic Gradient Descent (Shuffling SGD). A particularly popular strategy in Shuffling SGD is Random Reshuffling (RR), which has achieved great empirical success. Despite its strong performance, RR has long been considered a heuristic due to a lack of theoretical support. Over the last decade, people have finally established provable convergence rates for RR, thus justifying its observed superiority. However, for smooth convex optimization, two clouds over the convergence theory of RR remain. According to current theory, Shuffling SGD under RR converges only when the stepsize is smaller than a threshold proportional to $1/n$, where $n$ is the number of summands in the objective (or the number of data points). Consequently, the optimally tuned theoretical rate of Shuffling SGD under RR is strictly worse than that of SGD when the number of epochs is smaller than another threshold proportional to $n$. These two restrictions heavily limit the applicability of existing theories and leave a critical mismatch with practice. In this work, for the first time, we prove that RR dominates SGD in smooth convex optimization for any reasonable stepsize after any finite number of epochs, thereby addressing a longstanding open question. Moreover, we establish new algorithm-dependent lower bounds for RR and SGD, respectively. Altogether, these results yield (nearly) sharp worst-case characterizations of RR and SGD. Furthermore, we develop a shuffling-based method to optimize functions satisfying the quadratic growth condition, a strict relaxation of strong convexity, and derive a new complexity bound improving existing results proved under stronger assumptions.
item.dc:creator: Zijian Liu

item.title: A Bilevel Neurodynamic Approach for Distributed SCAD-Regularized Sparse Least Squares
item.description: arXiv:2611.07618v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper proposes a bilevel particle swarm optimization (PSO)-neurodynamic method for solving the distributed sparse least-squares problem regularized by the smoothly clipped absolute deviation (SCAD) penalty to global optimality. The SCAD penalty is nonsmooth and nonconvex, so existing distributed neurodynamic methods have not been extended to it directly. Through two-time-scale singular perturbation analysis, a rigorous full-trajectory convergence theory with explicit convergence rates is established for the inner collaborative multi-agent neurodynamic system without requiring the second-order sufficient condition. A theory-guided inner-outer collaborative optimization framework is further developed, in which a red-light green-light sensitivity mechanism is embedded in the outer PSO search to enhance global search while concentrating computational effort on the SCAD shape parameters, thereby improving recovery accuracy and computational efficiency. Simulation results on four sparse-recovery scenarios demonstrate that the proposed method accurately recovers the true sparsity pattern and achieves faster convergence and lower relative error than competing neurodynamic methods.
item.dc:creator: Juntao Li, Qihang Guo, Deyuan Meng

item.title: Projection-Free Gradient Tracking Neurodynamic for Distributed Nonnegative Sparse Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2611.07643v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper proposes a continuous-time, projection-free neurodynamic system based on gradient tracking for distributed nonnegative sparse optimization. Unlike traditional methods, our approach avoids projecting states onto the feasible set. Instead, it employs gradient tracking to estimate average gradients under heterogeneous costs, coupling primal and dual dynamics such that feasibility and sparsity emerge naturally from the equilibrium conditions. The system ensures unique solutions through a locally Lipschitz vector field and guarantees that every equilibrium corresponds to an exact KKT point. We establish rigorous convergence guarantees for convex objectives through three distinct analytical layers. These include a centralized kernel rate, a computable distributed rate derived from Jacobian analysis without restrictive stability assumptions, and a global exponential stability proof based on Lur'e system theory. Our analysis quantitatively separates these layers, revealing that the convergence rate is primarily limited by graph sparsity and remains robust to variations in momentum time scales. Numerical experiments on strongly convex quadratic problems validate the theoretical rates, demonstrate effective active set recovery, and show that the system maintains stable tail convergence rates even under strong local heterogeneity.
item.dc:creator: Juntao Li, Qihang Guo, Deyuan Meng

item.title: A Graph-Theoretic Approach to Matrix AM-GM: Counterexamples and Sharp Exponential Bounds
item.description: arXiv:2611.07649v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a graph-theoretic approach to the expected-norm matrix arithmetic--geometric mean inequality. By encoding matrix interactions with a path-supported Gram matrix, we obtain a projection family whose product is nonzero exactly when the transition graph of its index sequence is a path. This gives an intuitive explanation for failure: repeated indices can create cycles or branches that annihilate products, an effect absent for positive scalars. We prove the universal lower bound $(n)_m/n^m$ for the ratio of the with-replacement to the without-replacement mean and show that it is asymptotically sharp on the exponential scale when $m=n$. Specifically, our construction gives a ratio $\exp(-n+O(\sqrt n))$, matching the lower bound's leading exponential rate over unrestricted dimensions. We also determine an explicit overlap threshold, derive exact six-factor counterexamples, and show that exponential failure can coexist with vanishing pairwise commutators.
item.dc:creator: Zehua Liu

item.title: Randomized Parallel Complexity of Weakly Convex Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2611.07675v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the minimum number of query rounds needed to find approximate stationary points of nonsmooth weakly convex functions, measured by the gradient of the Moreau envelope. Each round permits multiple simultaneous queries. In the stated parameter regime, the standard subgradient rate is optimal in sufficiently high dimensions, even for randomized algorithms making polynomially many parallel queries per round. We then show how the order structure of the real line enables faster search: a deterministic algorithm using only function values achieves logarithmic round complexity, with a further reduction through parallel queries. Matching lower bounds hold even when each query returns the entire subdifferential. Together, these results clarify the role of dimension in determining the benefits of parallel queries for weakly convex optimization.
item.dc:creator: Kang Liu

item.title: Randomized and Oracle-Based Feasible Directions Methods for Nonsmooth Nonconvex Constrained Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2611.07691v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Minimizing nonsmooth nonconvex objectives over general convex sets using no derivatives of the objective, together with structural access to the constraint set, poses a fundamental geometric difficulty: at boundary points, the feasible direction cone may fail to be closed, preventing the construction of finite sets of search directions that capture all feasible descent directions. We develop a feasible-directions framework for problems structured as the difference between a continuously differentiable function and a convex function over a closed convex set, and access the objective without knowledge of its decomposition, through exact line searches along feasible segments. To address the geometric obstruction, we introduce $\eta$-feasible directions, which remain uniformly separated from the boundary of the feasible direction cone, enabling finite-direction search even in the presence of nonlinear constraints. We present two algorithmic realizations of this framework. The first assumes access to an $\eta$-direction oracle and extends feasible-directions methods from linear to general convex constraints. The second replaces the oracle by a noise-augmented randomization scheme that constructs spanning directions from the affine-hull inner normal and almost surely avoids nonsmooth boundary points when initialized outside that set. Under curvature bounds and Lipschitz continuity of the smooth component's gradient, we jointly control the spanning coefficients and feasible step lengths of the oracle construction. This yields finite-time approximate $d$-stationarity along every unit feasible direction admitting a prescribed positive step length. For both methods, we also establish a rate in the proximal directional minimization (PDM) measure, assuming uniformly bounded direction-set sizes. Randomized exploration ensures that, almost surely, every accumulation point is $d$-stationary.
item.dc:creator: Dan Greenstein, Nadav Hallak

item.title: Online Optimization for Controlling HVAC Systems
item.description: arXiv:2611.07777v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning (HVAC) systems account for a significant portion of buildings' energy consumption, motivating the design of energy- and cost-efficient control strategies. However, conventional strategies employ simple, reactive control, without incorporating a model. Therefore, in this paper we adopt an economic model predictive control framework and focus on designing online algorithms to solve the control input design problems with a limited computational budget. In particular, we propose two tailored online algorithms based on projected gradient descent, with a custom projection routine, and the projected primal-dual method. We discuss the pros and cons of both algorithm designs, focusing in particular on computational efficiency. We further compare them through numerical experiments simulating the control of an HVAC system over the course of a day. The results show that computationally efficient online solvers for HVAC systems control are indeed possible. Moreover, the performance closely matches that of a baseline algorithm with unlimited computational budget, in terms of reference temperature tracking and comfort temperature range enforcement.
item.dc:creator: Tong Wu, Dominik Baumann, Angela Fontan, Nicola Bastianello

item.title: Newton Steps are Faster for Linear Complementarity Problems
item.description: arXiv:2611.07815v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Linear Complementarity Problems (LCPs) with sufficient matrices form a well-studied class of problems, dating back from the foundational works of Cottle and Dantzig (1968). LCPs capture convex quadratic programs, and admit reductions from problems such as discounted stochastic games or mean-payoff games. While the original approach for solving these problems was based on pivoting methods, in their 1991 book, Kojima, Megiddo, Noma, and Yoshise introduced an interior point method (IPM) with running time that is polynomial in the input size, but which depends linearly on a certain parameter called the handicap number of the matrix. Despite the ensuing rich literature on sufficient LCP IPMs, the linear dependence on the handicap number has not been improved since then. We present an IPM whose running time depends on the square root of the handicap number. The algorithm can decrease the duality gap by a constant factor in $O\left(\min\left\{\sqrt{n} (1+\kappa),n^{9/8}\sqrt{1+\kappa}\right\}\right)$ iterations. Curiously, this can already be achieved using standard Newton updates. We analyze the IPM in a norm defined by a local weighting, where centralizing Newton steps quadratically converge to the central path, without any dependence on the handicap number. The weights arise from a characterization by Rump (Linear Algebra and Its Applications, 1997, 1998, 2003) of the sign-real spectral radius and its relation to sufficiency; another ingredient of our proof is a new operator norm characterization of the handicap number. Moreover, the connection to Rump's work also enables us to show coNP-completeness of testing sufficiency, and approximation hardness of the handicap number.
item.dc:creator: Haoyuan Ma, L\'aszl\'o A. V\'egh, Adrian Vladu

item.title: On the Spectral Dependence of Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Tracking
item.description:
arXiv:2611.07958v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study how the spectral geometry of the mixing matrix enters the convergence of decentralized stochastic gradient tracking (GT) for smooth strongly convex problems. General bounds contain the factor $\Delta_\lambda^{-3}$ in the higher-order stochastic term, where $\Delta_\lambda$ is the absolute spectral gap. We show that, even for two agents with identical quadratic objectives, the exact steady-state mean-square disagreement scales as $\alpha^2\sigma^2\Delta_\lambda^{-3}$ as the nontrivial eigenvalue approaches $-1$, provided the stepsize $\alpha$ is sufficiently small relative to the gap. Here $\sigma^2$ is the gradient-noise variance. By unrolling the disagreement recursion, we establish a stochastic bound that averages all nontrivial eigenvalue contributions for diagonalizable mixing matrices, up to an eigenvector conditioning factor. As a real or complex eigenvalue approaches the unit circle away from $1$, its contribution grows as the inverse cube of its distance to the circle; growth can be slower near $1$. For symmetric mixing with gaps $p$ at $1$ and $
u$ at $-1$, the weighted sum $	heta_1/p+	heta_2/
u^3$ replaces the prior factor $(\Delta_\lambda
u^2)^{-1}$. For $N$ agents, $N	heta_1$ and $N	heta_2$ count the nonnegative and negative nontrivial eigenvalues, respectively. On a symmetric family, a finite-horizon lower bound for the average iterate matches the worst-case factor $p^{-1}+
u^{-3}$ up to universal constants. Numerical experiments confirm the predicted scaling.
item.dc:creator: Sulaiman A. Alghunaim, Haoyuan Cai, Ali H. Sayed

item.title: Quantifying the remaining search space in analogue optimisation
item.description: arXiv:2611.07968v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Benchmarking analogue optimisers requires certifying not only how close a returned energy is to the optimum, but also how many better configurations may remain. Semidefinite relaxations provide rigorous bounds on the ground-state energy and selected observables, yet reveal little about the size of this residual search space. We introduce a deterministic, instance-specific upper bound on the number of binary configurations whose energies improve upon a returned state by a prescribed margin. Combined with a semidefinite energy interval, this yields a complementary certificate of both the magnitude and multiplicity of any possible improvement. To judge an analogue optimiser's native performance, we provide a generalisation of the framework to obtain bounds on the Haar volume of the remaining continuous phase-space. To further characterise the remaining search space, we extend our bounds to resolve regions in configuration space in both the binary and continuous setting. Our approach couples a variational-Chernoff reduction with an elimination bound of the resulting partition function. Comparisons with exact enumeration and independent Haar sampling are consistent with the bounds on small instances. In numerical experiments at $N=1000$, even the largest family-median bound restricts the potentially improving binary configurations to less than $10^{-144}$ of the full configuration space, while the largest upper bound on the corresponding Haar volume is of order $10^{-499}$.
item.dc:creator: Jona Nagerl, Younes Naceur, Natalia G. Berloff

item.title: Funnel MPC for port-Hamiltonian systems
item.description: arXiv:2611.08015v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Port-Hamiltonian systems are an energy-based modelling formalism, that has strong ties to the physical models and allows interconnection of systems. Funnel MPC, a Model Predictive Control (MPC) scheme, allows for output tracking with prescribed error bounds. Earlier works focused on systems with stable internal dynamics, which typically excludes port-Hamiltonian systems. We introduce a modified stage cost design that takes into account the port-Hamiltonian structure of the system and allows deactivation of the funnel cost. We show initial and recursive feasibility for a class of port-Hamiltonian systems with relative degree one including unstable internal dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Loris K\"onitzer, Jonas Kirchhoff, Thomas Berger

item.title: A globally convergent stochastic semismooth Newton method for strongly convex problems in Hilbert spaces
item.description: arXiv:2611.08061v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose and analyze a globalized stochastic semismooth Newton method for stochastic optimization problems in Hilbert spaces where the objective is strongly convex with Lipschitz continuous, Newton differentiable gradient. Gradient and generalized Hessian information are only available through mini-batching. In each iteration, a full semismooth Newton trial step is accepted or rejected based on a stochastic residual test and rejected steps are replaced by damped steps in the same Newton direction. Throughout, we admit gradient estimators with affinely growing variance, as arises in optimization problems with random partial differential equations as constraints. We prove non-asymptotic global R-linear convergence in expectation as well as almost sure convergence. For sufficiently fast-growing batch sizes, the method transitions almost surely into a regime of pure Newton steps and converges R-superlinearly almost surely. The method is applied to the optimal control of a random elliptic equation featuring a Huber tracking term as well as a random parabolic equation with a Moreau--Yosida penalization of an almost sure state constraint.
item.dc:creator: Pavel Dvurechensky, Caroline Geiersbach, Michael Hinterm\"uller, Felix Sauer

item.title: A Solution Method for Single-Source Capacitated Facility Location Problems Under Decision-Dependent Demand Uncertainty
item.description: arXiv:2611.08090v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a model and an exact solution method for single-source capacitated facility location problems with decision-dependent demand uncertainty. The model allows the joint probability distribution of customer demands to depend on the facility to which demand points are allocated. The number of possible decision-dependent distributions is therefore equal to the number of feasible allocations of demand points to (groups of) facilities. To address the exponential size of the model, we apply and extend a recent version of the L-Shaped method for stochastic programs with decision-dependent uncertainty. In particular,we compare the original optimality cut with a new optimality cut based on a bilinear reformulation. We prove that, separated together with the original one, the new cut yields a tighter restriction, at the expense of introducing bilinear terms. In addition, we prove an effective decision-independent valid inequality that significantly improves convergence. Extensive numerical tests on 180 instances demonstrate that the method, supported by the valid inequality, can find optimal or near-optimal solutions to problem instances with up to 620 potential probability distributions. The tests also show that, while the new cut closes slightly more instances, the original cut remains preferable in terms of solution time and optimality gap.
item.dc:creator: Giovanni Pantuso, Miguel Lejeune

item.title: Adaptive pairwise preference elicitation for decision support: identifying the best alternative with fewer judgments
item.description: arXiv:2611.08123v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Interactive decision support systems often require repeated preference judgments, although identifying the best alternative may not justify eliciting all \(n(n-1)/2\) pairwise comparisons. We propose ALEC (Adaptive Lexicographic Elicitation of Comparisons), which re-ranks the alternatives after each judgment and asks the first unobserved pair in the lexicographic order of the current ranking, using the Analytic Hierarchy Process as the concrete setting. Under a log-normal error model, directly comparing a contrast maximises the one-step reduction in its effective resistance. Posterior bounds on the probability of a wrong choice or of exceeding a relative-loss tolerance provide stopping rules valid under adaptive questioning, while a consistency-and-margin condition gives a deterministic certificate of agreement with the full-matrix winner. Simulations show that re-ranking is most useful in larger problems with limited budgets; ALEC outperforms Harker's original rule in most scenarios with \(n\ge11\), while under a common stopping rule it achieves higher hit-rate point estimates than the stronger Harker-log variant at a modest additional questioning cost. With a 5\% loss tolerance and a cap of \(2n\) additional comparisons, the stopping rule saves \res{prot-s06-saveadd-min}--\res{prot-s06-saveadd-max}\% of them, while among runs stopped by the bound the observed rate of losses above tolerance remains at most \res{s06-errearly-max}\%, against a nominal 10\%. ALEC therefore provides an adaptive elicitation module for decision support systems that balances decision precision against user effort.
item.dc:creator: Luis \'Angel Calvo, Jiri Mazurek

item.title: A Proximal Newton Framework with Local Superlinear Convergence for Simple Bilevel Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2611.08297v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we study a penalty method for simple bilevel optimization in which the lower-level objective has a convex composite structure. Our approach is based on a vanishing-penalty reformulation, which gives rise to a sequence of penalized problems as the penalty parameter decreases. A key difficulty is that metric subregularity of the lower-level optimality mapping does not, in general, yield a uniform error bound for the penalized problems as the penalty parameter vanishes, preventing a direct application of standard proximal Newton theory. To address this difficulty, we first analyze a regularized proximal Newton step by exploiting the specific structure of simple bilevel problems, and establish the local estimates that underpin superlinear convergence. Building on this local analysis, we propose SiB-Newton, which incorporates the proximal Newton step into a globalization strategy. We establish convergence guarantees for SiB-Newton and show that, under suitable local conditions, Newton steps are eventually accepted and the iterates converge at a superlinear rate. Numerical experiments on synthetic examples verify the predicted local superlinear convergence rate.
item.dc:creator: Xiaoning Bai, Boris S. Mordukhovich, Shangzhi Zeng, Jin Zhang

item.title: Hardness of integer linear feasibility with cyclic support
item.description: arXiv:2611.08304v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove that integer linear feasibility is strongly $NP$-complete even when the constraint matrix has exactly two nonzero entries in every row and column, with its support forming a single cycle. This holds already for monotone systems (one positive and one negative coefficient in each inequality) with nonzero coefficients of absolute value $2$ or $3$ and right-hand sides in $\{-1,0,1,2\}$. No variable bounds are supplied separately from the system. For systems in which each inequality involves at most two variables, this strengthens known hardness results by restricting all numerical data to fixed finite sets. For systems in which each variable occurs in at most two inequalities, this establishes, to the best of our knowledge, the first $NP$-hardness result for feasibility. We also give negative answers, unless $P=NP$, to questions on polynomial-time solvability of integer programs with bounded coefficients and bounded totally $\Delta$-modular treewidth, and on fixed-parameter tractability of integer bound propagation with respect to coefficient and right-hand-side magnitudes.
item.dc:creator: Marco Di Summa

item.title: A Theoretical Analysis of a Bilevel Optimization Formulation for Combined Local-Global Optical Flow Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.08359v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper analyzes a bilevel formulation for learning the regularization parameter of combined local-global (CLG) optical flow models. The lower-level problem computes the flow from a Lucas--Kanade data term and a quadratic or total variation (TV) regularizer, and the upper-level problem selects the parameter that minimizes the squared distance to a ground-truth flow. The setting is finite-dimensional, and a full-rank assumption makes the lower-level solution unique. For the quadratic model we derive sufficient conditions for the existence of an optimal parameter, for every optimal parameter to be positive, and for strict local optimality. For TV regularization an optimal parameter always exists, because the lower-level solution vanishes for large parameters, and we give a sufficient condition for positivity that accounts for the coupling of the two flow components through the local structure tensors. Synthetic examples illustrate the conditions, including cases in which they fail.
item.dc:creator: El Mostafa Kalmoun

item.title: Augmented Lagrangian methods with telescopic subproblems for MPCCs and cardinality constraints with general constraints: constraint-preserving swaps and B-stationarity
item.description: arXiv:2611.08404v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider optimization problems with general equality and inequality constraints and partitioned cardinality constraints, which include complementarity constraints. In the augmented Lagrangian method that we consider, the bounds and the cardinality constraints are kept in the subproblems, which are solved by the Telescopic Method. The limit points of this method are B-stationary, without constraint qualifications, if the penalty parameters remain bounded, but not in general. The reason is that the swaps of the Telescopic Method pass through points at which the constraints have different values, and the corresponding variation of the penalty term grows with the penalty parameter. With unbounded penalty parameters and a derivative test outside the current face, the feasible limit points at which a linear independence constraint qualification holds are M-stationary for MPCCs. We modify the swaps, by means of a scaled Newton restoration, so that they preserve the values of the constraints, and we prove that every feasible limit point at which this constraint qualification holds is then B-stationary (S-stationary for MPCCs), whatever the behavior of the penalty parameters. Counterexamples show that the modification is necessary, even with exact solutions of the subproblems, and that the constraint qualification cannot be weakened to one of Mangasarian-Fromovitz type. In the MacMPEC collection, the method found certified S- or B-stationary points in 185 of the 193 instances, more than Algencan and the regularization method of Scholtes. In experiments with cardinality-constrained portfolios and sparse principal component analysis, the constraint-preserving swaps improved the original swaps and the methods applied to complementarity reformulations.
item.dc:creator: Ernesto G. Birgin, J. M. Mart\'inez

item.title: An Accelerated Proximal Gradient Method for Bures-Wasserstein Space
item.description: arXiv:2611.08468v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study composite optimization over the Bures--Wasserstein (BW) space of Gaussian measures. Our main observation is that a useful class of BW problems can be lifted into the Euclidean space of affine transport maps, such that the lifted problems can be solved efficiently using accelerated proximal gradient methods. For objectives whose smooth and nonsmooth components admit convex smooth and convex proximable affine lifts, respectively, our algorithm BW-FISTA achieves minimax-optimal objective gap $O(k^{-2})$ after $k$ iterations. We verify these regularity conditions for potential and interaction energies together with common spectral regularizers, and we treat stochastic gradients under a suitable noise model. As a principal application, we consider Gaussian variational inference with a log-concave, log-smooth target. Here, the resulting entropy term is handled by an efficient, exact proximal step, and we improve the previous rate of $O(k^{-1})$ to $O(k^{-2})$. We numerically verify this predicted boost with synthetic experiments.
item.dc:creator: Jakob Nyl\"of, Sloan Nietert, Julien Pallage, Giancarlo Ferrari-Trecate, Daniel Kuhn, John Lygeros

item.title: The Computational Complexity of Avoiding Strict Saddle Points in Constrained Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2604.02285v2 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The complexity of finding second-order stationary points (SOSPs) in constrained settings has remained unclear and has been highlighted as an open question by the works of Hollender and Zampetakis [2023] and Kontogiannis et al. [2024]. In particular, under one established definition (SOSP1) where nonnegative curvature is required only along the null space of the active constraints [Bertsekas, 1997], the problem lies in TFNP, and algorithms with $O(poly(1/\epsilon))$ running times have been proposed. Under another established notion of stationarity (SOSP2) checking is coNP-hard in high dimensions. We investigate the computational landscape of finding SOSPs under polytope constraints. We prove that, even if promised that all KKT points lie a constant distance away from the domain's boundary--where SOSP1 and SOSP2 reduce to the standard unconstrained conditions--finding an approximate SOSP under either definition is PLS-hard, and the hardness continues to hold even in $[0,1]^2$. As a direct consequence, our result establishes a fundamental barrier on the continuity of SOSP-computing algorithms: unless PLS=CLS, no deterministic, iterative algorithm with a computationally efficient, continuous update rule can guarantee that every $\epsilon$-approximate fixed point is an $(\epsilon,\sqrt{\epsilon})$-SOSP, even under the above interior promise. We establish PLS-completeness by proving that the problem of finding approximate SOSP1 belongs to PLS in high dimensions. In addition, we prove that, for every fixed $d\ge 2$, finding an approximate SOSP2 is also PLS-complete, escaping the coNP-hardness which appears in high dimensions. We also establish PLS-hardness and a polynomial-time search reduction to LOCALOPT for finding $(r^{2+\gamma},r)$-local pure Nash equilibria, for every fixed rational $\gamma\in(0,1]$, in two-player nonconvex common-interest games with actions in $[0,1]$.
item.dc:creator: Andreas Kontogiannis, Ioannis Panageas, Vasilis Pollatos

item.title: Distributed Geometric Optimization and Control of Rigid Differential-Drive Formations from Relative-Position Measurements
item.description: arXiv:2611.07163v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Distance based formation control fixes the shape of a robot team but leaves its position and orientation unconstrained. We regulate all three for differential drive robots that have only one absolute position anchor, absolute headings, body frame relative position measurements, and communication with their neighbors. We derive a two layer estimation control scheme directly from optimization. The first half of the result is a set of graph-proximal estimators that reconstruct the centroid, the anchor vector, and the centered coordinates. Exact proximal updates reach consensus in finitely many steps, and a finite number of primal dual iterations leaves a bounded reconstruction error. The controller combines proximal centroid and orientation steps with distance gradient shape regulation, and a finite rotation removes the orientation drift caused by the shape step. A discrete Lyapunov analysis gives local exponential convergence once the estimators have converged. We validate the method in ROS 2 Gazebo and in experiments with five physical robots.
item.dc:creator: Thanacha Choopojcharoen, Erman Selim, Ramisha Anjum, Baris Fidan

item.title: Exact penalties for maximum-edge bicliques in bipartite graphs
item.description: arXiv:2611.07239v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Given a bipartite graph $G$, we denote by $g(G)$ the largest product $|A||B|$ over pairs of vertex sets $A$ and $B$, one on each side, with no edge between them. These pairs are the bicliques of the bipartite complement of $G$; hence, computing $g(G)$ is the maximum-edge biclique problem, which is NP-hard, as shown by Peeters in 2003. Gillis and Glineur characterized it by a continuous quadratic program, in which a large enough penalty on the edges of $G$ makes the global maximizers correspond to the maximum pairs and the local maximizers to the maximal ones. We propose a new threshold for the penalty, which depends only on $g(G)$. For any penalty at or above it, the global maximizers correspond exactly to the maximum pairs, and every local maximizer with positive value corresponds to a maximal pair. This threshold is never larger than theirs and is sharp up to an additive $1/2$. Spectral and semidefinite bounds give computable penalties; in experiments, a simple local ascent succeeds far more often with the semidefinite one than with the earlier thresholds, although on our graphs that bound already reveals $g(G)$. The penalty formulation, whose optimal value is $\sqrt{g(G)}/2$, is also a copositive formulation of $g(G)$. Strengthening a semidefinite bound of Laurent, Polak and Vargas with the completely positive cone gives exactly $\sqrt{g(G)}/2$, while the doubly nonnegative strengthening is already inexact on six vertices. Finally, P\'olya's linear programming approximations of the copositive cone become finite at an explicit level and converge to $\sqrt{g(G)}/2$ without ever being exact.
item.dc:creator: Youssouf Emine, Bissan Ghaddar

item.title: Truncated backpropagation through time induces a two-sided gradient turnpike property
item.description: arXiv:2611.07415v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Truncated backpropagation through time reduces the computational burden of training recurrent models by restricting gradient computations to shorter temporal contexts. This induces two distinct boundary effects: missing past information perturbs the forward state evolution, while truncating the backward recursion omits future information. This motivates decoupling the interval over which gradient contributions are averaged for the parameter update from the surrounding temporal context over which they are computed. Under exponential decay of the state-transition Jacobians and mild regularity conditions, this leads to a two-sided gradient turnpike property: the error between truncated- and full-context gradient contributions decays exponentially with the distance from both context boundaries. We derive bounds for the averaged update gradient, yielding guarantees on gradient alignment and approximate full-context stationarity; under unbiased interval sampling and a Polyak-Lojasiewicz condition, these further imply a bound on the resulting optimality gap. Numerical experiments on the Wiener-Hammerstein benchmark illustrate the role of past and future context and the trade-off between predictive performance and computational cost.
item.dc:creator: Julian D. Schiller, Matthias A. M\"uller

item.title: Learning and Steering in Incomplete-Information Games
item.description: arXiv:2611.07589v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In many modern multi-agent systems, a mediator seeks to influence strategic decision dynamics using only outcome-level feedback and without knowing agents' utilities. In this work, we study how a mediator can learn an unknown game and steer adaptive agents toward outcomes that maximize her utility using only trajectory feedback. The mediator knows the game form and her own objective, but not the agents' utilities. Moreover, she commits to nonnegative payments and provides recommendations and contexts, but receives only a single realized terminal outcome rather than full-information feedback. We develop halving-type algorithms that learn utility differences in normal-form games and conditional continuation-value differences in extensive-form games, achieving a sample complexity of $\widetilde O(\varepsilon^{-2})$ that matches worst-case lower bounds up to logarithmic factors. We then combine these learning procedures with a Lagrangian formulation in an online Learn-Compute-Steer algorithm that interleaves learning, equilibrium computation, and steering toward mediator-optimal extensive-form correlated equilibria (EFCE). With high probability, the Learn-Compute-Steer algorithm achieves a directness gap and an optimality gap of $\widetilde O(T^{-1/4})$, while time-average payments are of $\widetilde O(T^{-1/8})$.
item.dc:creator: Asr{\i}n Efe Yorulmaz, Tamer Ba\c{s}ar

item.title: Quantifying and minimizing collision intensity in stationary crowd flow
item.description: arXiv:2611.07837v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We develop a continuum model to quantify kinematic collision risk in stationary crowd flow. From the density-weighted inward relative flux, we derive a collision functional based on the symmetric velocity gradient. For incompressible flows with constant density, this functional is convex and positively homogeneous of degree one in a combination of second derivatives of the stream function. We minimize it subject to prescribed boundary flux. On bounded simply connected domains with Lipschitz boundary, under a finite-energy lifting assumption, we prove existence of minimizers in a relaxed class that allows this derivative combination to be a vector-valued Radon measure. We show that disks are the only domains with a nontrivial zero-trace kernel, corresponding to rigid rotation about the center. Using the compact embedding for functions of bounded deformation, we prove that relaxed energy sublevels are compact without normalization on every other admissible domain, and after removing one rotational component on disks. We identify the relaxed functional with the strong $W^{1,1}$ lower semicontinuous envelope of the functional on the prescribed-trace class with integrable controlled derivatives. Then, we derive optimality conditions via convex duality. We construct explicit radial flows on annular sectors and prove that they minimize the energy over the full admissible classes, including nonradial competitors. On the square, distinct minimizers with the same prescribed boundary flux have different local collision intensities. The square--disk comparison shows that the saddle flow loses optimality when the domain changes, even after normalization.
item.dc:creator: Yuri Ashrafyan, Diogo A. Gomes

item.title: XM4D: 4D Reconstruction through Certifiable Geometric Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2611.07902v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Accurate 4D reconstruction remains challenging: jointly estimating camera motion, scene geometry, and non-rigid deformation entails highly nonconvex optimization, making global optimality difficult to guarantee. We present XM4D, a framework for accurate and efficient 4D reconstruction built upon certifiably globally optimal geometric optimization. By separating the estimation of camera motion from non-rigid deformation, we formulate both stages as structured quadratically constrained quadratic programs (QCQP) that admit semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxations and verifiable global optimality certificates. For camera motion estimation, we lift static point tracks into 3D using foundational depth prediction models and formulate a scaled bundle adjustment problem that jointly estimates camera poses, depth scales, and static landmarks. By analytically eliminating translations and landmarks, we reduce the problem to a QCQP over scaled rotations. For non-rigid reconstruction, we represent dynamic motion using an embedded deformation graph (EDG) and show that its tracking, rigidity, and temporal regularization objectives similarly reduce to a rotation-only QCQP. Both problems admit SDP relaxations that we solve efficiently with a GPU-accelerated Burer-Monteiro solver based on Riemannian optimization. The recovered geometry further initializes dynamic Gaussian splatting for photometric refinement. Extensive experiments across seven benchmarks demonstrate accurate camera motion estimation on both static and dynamic scenes, efficient optimization that scales to thousands of frames, and state-of-the-art novel-view rendering quality.
item.dc:creator: Haoyu Han, Jack Benarroch Jedlicki, Jiahui Lei, Heng Yang

item.title: Reversible Dynamics, Asymmetric Actions: Parking as a Trajectory-Level Affordance
item.description: arXiv:2611.07965v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Drivers are often told to back into a tight parking space, not drive in nose first. The advice looks paradoxical, because a slow car is dynamically reversible: reverse its speed and replay the steering backward, and it retraces a feasible path. Played backward, though, reverse-in shows a car driving forward out of the space. Reverse-in and forward-in are different tasks: they share a start position but end facing opposite ways. We separate three clearances between car and obstacles. Static fit $F$ is the clearance the parked car keeps at its best acceptable destination pose. Eventual access $A_\infty$ is the clearance it can keep all the way there with unlimited corrections. Resource-bounded access $A_K$ is the clearance that survives a budget of $K$ reversals, switches between forward and reverse. They satisfy $F\ge A_\infty\ge A_K$. In one fully specified scene (one car, bay, aisle and start), a certified argument proves $A_\infty=F=0.5000$ m for both tasks. In this scene, all certified forward/reverse asymmetry therefore arises at finite $K$: it lies in how many corrections each task needs, not in the clearance either can eventually keep. With one reversal, an explicit path gives reverse-in at least $0.4410$ m clearance. A certified reachability argument caps forward-in's one-reversal clearance at $d_0<0.1720002$ m. With two reversals, forward-in gets at least $0.2833$ m. To keep a clearance strictly above any $d$ with $d_0\le d<0.2833$ m, reverse-in thus needs exactly one reversal and forward-in exactly two when both tasks move forward first. If both move in reverse first, the counts are two and three. The contrast depends on the start position (Section 4.15). Proposed experiments test whether observers distinguish fit, eventual access and budgeted access. They compare these with simpler cues, such as how the turning body sweeps, and learned manoeuvre labels.
item.dc:creator: Adam Y. Shavit

item.title: On the Minimal Controllability of Boolean Networks With $k$-Regular Dependency Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2611.08101v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Boolean networks (BNs) are widely used to model gene regulatory networks and other biological systems. In this paper, we investigate the minimal controllability problem for BNs subject to degree constraints. We first establish three new best-case upper bounds for XOR-BNs whose dependency graphs are $k$-regular. We then introduce classes of BNs that are invariant under cyclically partite transformation (CPT-invariant) and prove theorems connecting BN controllability with the surjectivity of vector-valued Boolean functions. Finally, by combining an analysis of this surjectivity with a probabilistic argument, we derive a new general lower bound on the minimum number of control nodes required for majority-type threshold BNs with $(2k+1)$-regular dependency graphs.
item.dc:creator: Christopher H. Fok, Chi-Wing Wong, Wai-Ki Ching

item.title: Overcoming Fundamental Control Limitations in Powered Descent Flight through Robust Incremental Nonlinear Dynamic Inversion
item.description: arXiv:2611.08121v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This work identifies a fundamental, controller-independent limitation in reusable launch vehicle powered descent: a sudden $180^\circ$ phase transition in the open-loop transfer functions from the control inputs to the lateral drift and drift rate. The transition occurs inside the flight envelope, reverses the effective control direction, and can destabilize the closed loop system under uncertainty. An analytical condition governing this transition is derived, its physical mechanism is established, and its dependence on vehicle mass, aerodynamic properties, and geometry is characterized. An Incremental Nonlinear Dynamic Inversion (INDI)-based control architecture is then developed to inherently address this limitation and is tuned via $\mathcal{H}_\infty$ Closed Loop Shaping to provide local robustness and performance guarantees. The internal dynamics introduced by the INDI inversion are analytically derived and proven to be stable throughout the flight envelope. The proposed controller is compared against a robust gain-scheduled baseline controller through linear stability analysis and an extensive nonlinear Monte Carlo campaign. Both controllers achieve 100% success across the considered Monte Carlo campaign, though the INDI-based controller provides improved tracking performance, superior nominal and dispersed stability margins, requires fewer controller design points, and reduces controller tuning complexity.
item.dc:creator: Jo\~ao T. Diz, Paulo Rosa, Pedro Simpl\'icio, Paul Acquatella, Erik-Jan van Kampen, Spilios Theodoulis

item.title: Viscosity-variational inequality solutions of fully nonlinear second-order stationary mean field games with nonseparable and nondifferentiable Hamiltonians
item.description: arXiv:2611.08201v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We analyse stationary fully nonlinear uniformly elliptic second-order mean field games with nonseparable and nondifferentiable Hamiltonians by introducing the notion of viscosity-variational inequality solution. In this formulation of the problem, the value function is the viscosity solution of the Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman (HJB) equation, and the Kolmogorov--Fokker--Planck (KFP) equation for the player density is understood as a nonstandard variational inequality that no longer involves partial derivatives of the value function. The advantages of this formulation are found in its stability and continuity properties for handling weak convergence arguments, which we use to prove the existence of solutions of the problem. Furthermore, we prove the equivalence of the notion of viscosity-variational inequality solution with the notion of a partial differential inclusion solution, where the value function is a strong solution of the HJB equation and the player density is a very weak solution of the KFP equation with coefficients belonging to subdifferential sets of the Hamiltonian. Finally, we prove the uniqueness of solutions in the case of separable Hamiltonians with strictly monotone couplings.
item.dc:creator: Thomas Sales, Iain Smears

item.title: All minimum cuts of symmetric submodular functions
item.description: arXiv:2611.08253v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We compute Cunningham's canonical decomposition of a symmetric submodular function on $n$ elements in $O(n^3)$ time. The decomposition represents all minimum cuts in linear space. For the pair $s,t$ produced by Queyranne's algorithm, we construct in $O(n^2)$ time a digraph representing exactly the minimum $st$-cuts of the function. Using this construction in Chekuri and Xu's decomposition algorithm gives the cubic bound.
item.dc:creator: Chao Xu

item.title: Dynamic Optimistic Constrained OCO with Memory via Delay Equivalence
item.description: arXiv:2611.08302v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Online Convex Optimization with memory and time-varying constraints (COCO-M) is a recently-introduced framework that captures the dynamics of stateful online learning and non-stochastic control with budget constraints. Despite its expressive power, COCO-M remains largely understudied. In this work, we tackle this problem in its full scale, providing an optimistic algorithm that incorporates untrusted predictions to tame universal dynamic regret and cumulative constraint violation. Our analysis leverages a potent reduction from memory to delay and treats state-dependent gradients as delayed feedback. We establish the first bounds that adapt to both environment non-stationarity (path length $P_T$) and prediction accuracy, while lifting previous restrictive assumptions such as functional separability. En route to these results, we derive findings of independent interest for the memory-to-delay reduction, and for delayed OCO with time-varying constraints. The proposed framework ensures sublinear worst-case guarantees that improve with prediction accuracy, reaching $\mathcal O(1)$ regret under perfect predictions, with cumulative constraint violation (CCV) $\mathcal O(\sqrt{T})$ for unknown $P_T$ and $\mathcal O(\log T)$ for known or online observable $P_T$ , while recovering the optimal COCO rates when memory disappears.
item.dc:creator: Mohammed Abdullah, George Iosifidis, Salah Eddine Elayoubi, Tijani Chahed

item.title: Adversarial Training with Large Step Sizes: Implicit Bias, Optimization, and Sharpness
item.description: arXiv:2611.08457v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Adversarial Training (AT) is an important method for improving model robustness. We study the dynamics of deterministic Gradient Descent (GD) in AT. Most existing works in this direction focus on the small or vanishing step sizes regime, where GD resembles a continuous-time flow. However, such step sizes can make training inefficient and are rarely used in practice. In this paper, we study the AT dynamics of GD with large constant step sizes. We first study GD in adversarial linear logistic regression, focusing on two aspects: where the model parameters converge (implicit bias) and how quickly the losses decrease (optimization). We then turn to neural networks training and study how the sharpness of losses evolve during AT. Our results advance the understanding of the behaviors of GD with large step sizes in AT and highlight three key differences from its behavior in Standard Training (ST): (i) the implicit bias gap between AT and ST, previously established only for small step sizes, persists for arbitrarily large constant step sizes, (ii) different from ST, there is no uniform rate of convergence for the optimization error in AT, and (iii) sharpness can exhibit two-stage dynamics that differ from the Edge-of-Stability behavior observed in ST.
item.dc:creator: Yi Feng, Andrea Paudice

item.title: Distributionally Robust Airport Ground Holding Problem under Wasserstein Ambiguity Sets
item.description: arXiv:2306.09836v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop a distributionally robust formulation of the single-airport ground holding problem (dr-SAGHP) using a $1$-Wasserstein ambiguity set with an $\ell_1$ transportation metric over the full physical capacity support. We exploit the problem's structural properties to develop an exact dynamic programming separation algorithm within delayed constraint generation (DCG-DP). We also develop K-IL, which combines Kelley's cutting-plane method with an integer L-shaped framework to solve a a restricted-support approximation, rs-dr-SAGHP. Delayed constraint generation with MILP separation (DCG-MILP) serves as the computational baseline. Computational experiments demonstrate substantial runtime reductions for DCG-DP and K-IL relative to this baseline. Airport capacity distributions are constructed using Gaussian process regression based on historical weather and operational data at Denver International Airport from 2021 to 2023. We develop a chronological expanding-window calibration procedure to select the Wasserstein radius and the results show that the calibrated dr-SAGHP approaches reduce mean operational cost by approximately $2.6\%$ and the Conditional Value at Risk $\mathrm{CVaR}_{90}$ by approximately $8\%$ relative to the stochastic SAGHP benchmark, while avoiding the excessive conservatism observed in a classical robust optimization benchmark.
item.dc:creator: Haochen Wu, Alexander S. Estes, Max Z. Li

item.title: Mirror Descent-Ascent for mean-field min-max problems
item.description: arXiv:2402.08106v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study two variants of the mirror descent-ascent (MDA) algorithm for solving min-max problems on the space of measures: simultaneous and alternating. We work under assumptions of convexity-concavity and relative smoothness of the payoff function with respect to a suitable Bregman divergence, defined on the space of measures via flat derivatives. We establish non-asymptotic convergence rates to mixed Nash equilibria, measured in the Nikaid\^{o}-Isoda error, proving an $\mathcal{O}(N^{-1/2})$ rate for simultaneous MDA and an improved $\mathcal{O}(N^{-2/3})$ rate for alternating MDA. The main technical contribution is an infinite-dimensional dual space analysis that relates Bregman divergences on measures to dual Bregman divergences on spaces of bounded continuous functions, allowing us to control asymmetric commutator terms created by alternating updates. The results substantially generalize prior analyses restricted to bilinear objectives and also apply to nonlinear convex-concave problems on measure spaces, thereby providing a unified theoretical foundation for MDA in mean-field min-max optimization.
item.dc:creator: Razvan-Andrei Lascu, Mateusz B. Majka, {\L}ukasz Szpruch

item.title: Q-Learning under Finite Model Uncertainty
item.description: arXiv:2407.04259v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We propose a robust Q-learning algorithm for Markov decision processes under model uncertainty when each state--action pair is associated with a finite ambiguity set of candidate transition kernels. This finite-measure framework enables user-designed uncertainty models, including competing fitted models and stress scenarios. {The learner observes successor states and their deterministic rewards from every candidate simulator, without requiring explicit knowledge of the transition probabilities or the reward function.} We establish almost sure convergence of the learned Q-function to the robust optimum, and derive a time-uniform high-probability error certificate that separates an observable empirical Bellman residual from transition-kernel estimation error. We also give quantitative finite-ambiguity approximation results for Wasserstein and parametric uncertainty models on finite state spaces. Numerical examples illustrate the effect of scenario selection and compare the tabular algorithm with robust value iteration.
item.dc:creator: Julian Sester, C\'ecile Decker

item.title: A Bregman-Sinkhorn Algorithm for the Maximum Weight Independent Set Problem
item.description: arXiv:2408.02086v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We propose a scalable approximate algorithm for the NP-hard maximum-weight independent set problem, based on dual coordinate descent applied to a smoothed clique-cover LP relaxation. Our method, a variant of the Bregman/Sinkhorn algorithm, employs entropy smoothing with a novel duality-gap-based smoothing scheduling strategy that empirically outperforms standard feasibility scheduling for the relaxed problem. Our new projection to the primal feasible set enables accurate duality gap estimation. Combined with a basic primal heuristic leveraging reduced costs, our approach yields high-quality integer solutions. On real-world datasets, it efficiently finds high-quality approximate solutions for graphs with up to 882,000 nodes and 344 million edges within seconds.
item.dc:creator: Stefan Haller, Bogdan Savchynskyy

item.title: SAGE: A Set-based Adaptive Gradient Estimator
item.description: arXiv:2508.19400v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce a set membership perspective on gradient estimation for black-box scalar functions, in which the gradient is not approximated as a single point estimate but characterised as a member of a set of admissible gradients consistent with available function samples and regularity assumptions. Bounds on gradient uncertainty, obtained from standard multivariate Taylor series results, are used to represent this admissible set through linear inequalities, making gradient uncertainty explicit and directly exploitable. Building on this formulation, we propose an adaptive strategy to refine the admissible gradient set to a desired precision by selectively acquiring new samples only when necessary. The resulting framework naturally accommodates function evaluations affected by noise with finite but a priori unknown bounds, yields the theoretical best attainable precision of the gradient set, and provides the optimal sampling distance from the point of interest to maximise information gain during refinement. Within this framework, we introduce the Set-Based Adaptive Gradient Estimator (SAGE), which extracts an estimate of the true gradient from the admissible set whilst preserving high sample efficiency and robustness to noise. Numerical experiments on large collections of random gradient-query points, as well as in the context of a first-order optimisation method, compared the performance of SAGE against commonly used gradient estimators from the literature. Our results show that SAGE achieved competitive gradient accuracy across noise levels without requiring any a priori noise characterisation. In a first-order optimisation setting, noise-informed competitors can outperform SAGE when such characterisation is available. Nevertheless, SAGE remained broadly competitive, making it particularly attractive in settings where noise characterisation is impractical to obtain.
item.dc:creator: Lorenzo Sabug Jr., Fredy Ruiz, Lorenzo Fagiano

item.title: Bridging Batch and Streaming Estimations to System Identification under Adversarial Attacks
item.description: arXiv:2509.15794v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: System identification in modern engineering systems faces emerging challenges from unanticipated adversarial attacks beyond existing detection mechanisms. In this work, we obtain a provably accurate estimate of the Markov parameter matrix of order $k$ to identify partially observed linear systems, in which the probability $p$ of having an attack at each time is smaller than $0.5$. We show that given the batch data accumulated up to time $T^*$, the $\ell_2$-norm estimator achieves an error with stepwise exponential decay as the attack probability $p$ decreases. Furthermore, low-dimensional attack structures can decouple the exponential decay order from the attack probability $p$, achieving an error decay that scales with $T^*$. We then propose a stochastic projected subgradient descent algorithm on streaming data that produces an estimate at each time $t<T^*$, in which case the expected estimation error proves to be the larger of $\mathcal{O}(k/\sqrt{t})$ and the baseline error of the $\ell_2$-norm estimator at $T^*$. This stochastic approach illustrates how non-smooth estimators can leverage first-order methods despite lacking recursive formulas. Finally, we integrate batch and streaming estimations to recover the Hankel matrix using the appropriate estimates of the Markov parameter matrix, which enables the synthesis of a robust adaptive controller based on the estimated balanced truncated model under adversarial attacks.
item.dc:creator: Jihun Kim, Javad Lavaei

item.title: Boscia.jl: A review and tutorial
item.description: arXiv:2511.01479v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Mixed-integer nonlinear optimization (MINLP) comprises a large class of problems that are challenging to solve and exhibit a wide range of structures. The Boscia framework (Hendrych et al., 2025b) focuses on convex MINLP where the nonlinearity appears in the objective only. This paper provides an overview of the framework, showcases extensions post-publication and practical examples to illustrate its use and customizability. One key aspect is the integration and exploitation of Frank-Wolfe methods as continuous solvers within a branch-and-bound framework, enabling inexact node processing, warm-starting and explicit use of combinatorial structure among others. Three examples illustrate its flexibility, the user control over the optimization process and the benefit of oracle-based access to the objective and its gradient. Additionally, ablation studies are performed on the three examples to investigate the performance impact of the different features and customizations. The aim of this tutorial is to provide readers with an understanding of the main principles of the framework.
item.dc:creator: Wenjie Xiao, Deborah Hendrych, Mathieu Besan\c{c}on, Sebastian Pokutta

item.title: Convergence and Stability of a Catching-Up Algorithm for Differential Inclusions with Maximally Monotone Operators
item.description: arXiv:2604.10774v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study a catching-up algorithm with approximate projections for finite-dimensional differential inclusions governed by a maximally monotone operator and a continuous perturbation. Through the canonical decomposition of the operator into a regular part and the normal cone to the closure of its domain, the problem becomes a sweeping process, discretized by an explicit predictor step and a feasible approximate projection. For variable time steps, the approximations converge, up to a subsequence, to a solution on every finite horizon when the mesh size and the accumulated projection-error budget vanish and the nodes stay in a common compact convex set. This set comes from linear growth on finite horizons and, without any growth condition, by dissipativity of the projected field at a feasible center, which confines the nodes to a fixed ball uniformly in time for small steps and small projection errors. Under either condition, locally Lipschitz perturbations give global well-posedness, convergence of the whole family, and, for a common initial state, a trajectory-error estimate of order $O(\sqrt{h+E})$, where $h$ is the maximal step and $E$ the accumulated budget; sparse projection errors are allowed. An elastic network with unilateral stops illustrates the results, and numerical experiments compare the algorithm with the full-resolvent discretization.
item.dc:creator: Tan H. Cao, Hassan Saoud

item.title: Symplectic Inductive Bias for Data-Driven Target Reachability in Hamiltonian Systems
item.description: arXiv:2604.17213v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Inductive bias refers to restrictions on the hypothesis class that enable a learning method to generalize effectively from limited data. A canonical example in control is linearity, which underpins low sample-complexity guarantees for stabilization and optimal control. For general nonlinear dynamics, by contrast, guarantees often rely on smoothness assumptions (e.g., Lipschitz continuity) which, when combined with covering arguments, can lead to data requirements that grow exponentially with the ambient dimension. In this paper we argue that data-efficient nonlinear control demands exploiting inductive bias embedded in nature itself, namely, structure imposed by physical laws. Focusing on Hamiltonian systems, we leverage symplectic geometry and intrinsic recurrence on energy level sets to solve target reachability problems.
